intuition.summary: Dedekind domains are where unique factorization is restored at the level of ideals: elements may factor non-uniquely, but every nonzero ideal is uniquely a product of prime ideals. The class group measures exactly how far elements are from ideals.
intuition.source: Gathmann, Commutative Algebra, Ch.13 (Prop. 13.7, Prop. 13.27); Wikipedia 'Ideal class group'

intuition.summary: Locally a Dedekind domain is as simple as possible: each localisation at a nonzero prime is a DVR, a 'simple UFD' whose ideals are powers of one uniformizer. Global questions are reduced to these local ones and glued back via A = intersection of A_p.
intuition.source: Aitken arXiv:2102.11725 §2, §7; Sutherland 18.785 Lecture 2 Prop. 2.6, Cor. 2.7

intuition.summary: Geometric picture: maximal ideals are points of a smooth curve, the valuation v_p(f) is the order of vanishing of f at p, and the factorisation of (f) is the divisor of zeros of f. Dedekind = coordinate ring of a smooth affine curve; Pic records divisors modulo divisors of functions.

In a Dedekind domain 'to contain is to divide', so ideals behave like numbers in reverse order: bigger ideals are smaller divisors, I+J is the gcd and the intersection is the lcm, and valuations combine by min/max/addition.
intuition.source: Sutherland Lecture 3 footnote 2; Gathmann Prop. 13.13; Conrad 'Ideal factorization' §4

intuition.summary: Ideal group as a free abelian group: a nonzero fractional ideal is just a finitely supported vector of exponents (v_p(I))_p, so multiplication is addition of exponent vectors.

Dedekind domains are 'almost PIDs': every ideal needs at most two generators, and one of them can be chosen to be any given nonzero element ('one and a half generators'). Semilocal Dedekind domains are PIDs.
intuition.source: Sutherland Lecture 3 Thm 3.22, Cor. 3.21; Conrad Thm 4.11; Gathmann Prop. 13.14

motivation.summary: Kummer introduced 'ideal complex numbers' to repair failed unique factorisation in cyclotomic integers while studying higher reciprocity (and Fermat's Last Theorem, per Wikipedia); his theory needed case-by-case choices.
motivation.source: Corry, 'Steht es alles wirklich schon bei Dedekind?' (2017) §2-3; Wikipedia 'Dedekind domain' History

motivation.summary: Dedekind (supplements to Dirichlet's Vorlesungen, versions 1871, 1877/79, 1894) replaced ideal numbers by sets closed under addition and multiplication by ring elements, chose the ring of all algebraic integers of a field as the right domain, and later built a full arithmetic of ideals with products and inverses.

Noether's axiomatic ideal theory (1921, 1927 'Abstrakter Aufbau der Idealtheorie') identified the abstract rings in which ideals factor uniquely; these are now called Dedekind domains. Hilbert's Zahlbericht (1897) had popularised Dedekind's conceptual approach.
Gauss's composition of binary quadratic forms gave the first class groups; Dedekind's ideal class group generalises this (with the narrow class group matching forms for real quadratic fields).
motivation.source: Wikipedia 'Ideal class group' (History; narrow class group)

motivation.summary: Two motivating families: rings of integers of number fields and coordinate rings of smooth curves were the first important examples, which is why the notion sits between number theory and algebraic geometry.

definitions.summary: Primary definition in many texts: a noetherian, integrally closed domain of Krull dimension <= 1 (often: every nonzero prime is maximal). This is the definition usually checked in practice.
definitions.source: Baanen et al. arXiv:2102.02600 §5.1; Wikipedia (DD4); Stacks Lemma 10.120.17(3)

definitions.summary: Local definition: a noetherian domain whose localisation at every nonzero prime is a DVR. Equivalence with (noetherian, integrally closed, dim <= 1) uses that integral closure and dimension are local, and that a 1-dimensional noetherian integrally closed local domain is a DVR.
Gathmann defines Dedekind as a 1-dimensional noetherian domain whose localisations at maximal ideals are regular local rings, and shows (Lemma 13.3) this is equivalent to being normal.

Stacks Project defines a Dedekind domain as a domain in which every nonzero ideal is a product of nonzero primes, uniquely up to order (no noetherian hypothesis), and proves equivalence with the noetherian-normal-dim<=1 and DVR-localisation definitions.

Invertibility definition: every nonzero (fractional) ideal is invertible. Proof that it implies noetherian: from I I^{-1} = A write 1 = sum a_i b_i with a_i in I, b_i in I^{-1}; then the a_i generate I.
definitions.source: Baanen et al. §5.3 (following Fröhlich); Sutherland Lecture 3 Lemma 3.4

definitions.summary: Eight equivalent characterisations: integrally closed noetherian dim<=1; noetherian with DVR localisations; nonzero ideals invertible; nonzero ideals are products of primes; noetherian and contain=divide; every ideal has J with IJ principal; every proper quotient a principal ideal ring; I=(a,b) for any nonzero a in I.

Fractional ideal: finitely generated A-submodule of K = Frac A (Sutherland), or an A-submodule I with dI contained in A for some nonzero d (Conrad, Gathmann, mathlib); these agree for noetherian A (Sutherland Lemma 2.14). Inverse candidate (A:I) = {x in K : xI in A}; I invertible iff I(A:I)=A.
definitions.source: Sutherland Lecture 2 Def. 2.13, Lemma 2.14, Lemma 2.20; Conrad §2; Gathmann Def. 13.15

definitions.summary: Invertibility is local: I is invertible iff I_m is invertible for all maximal m; in a noetherian local domain invertible = principal, so in a noetherian domain invertible = locally principal (= locally free of rank 1).
definitions.source: Sutherland Lecture 3 Thm 3.2, Lemma 3.4, Cor. 3.5; Stacks Lemma 10.120.16

definitions.summary: Class group: Cl(A) = (invertible fractional ideals)/(nonzero principal fractional ideals), defined for any domain, also written Pic(A); for Dedekind A every nonzero fractional ideal is invertible. Cl trivial iff PID iff UFD.
definitions.source: Sutherland Lecture 2 Def. 2.22-2.23, Lecture 3 Cor. 3.15; Baanen et al. §8.1

definitions.summary: Ring of integers O_K: integral closure of Z in a number field K (of F_q[t] in a function field); it is Dedekind because the integral closure of a Dedekind domain in a finite separable extension is Dedekind (trace pairing gives finite generation; integral extension preserves dim<=1). Separability can be dropped via Krull-Akizuki.
definitions.source: Sutherland 2015 Lecture 4 Thm 4.63, Rem. 4.61, 4.64; Baanen et al. §7; Stacks Lemma 10.120.18

definitions.summary: Unique factorisation proof routes: (a) local: ideal group is free on primes via valuations v_p(I) (Sutherland); (b) invertibility of primes + every ideal contains a product of primes + cancellation (Conrad, mathlib); (c) primary decomposition: p-primary ideals are powers of p (Gathmann).
definitions.source: Sutherland Lecture 3 Thm 3.11; Conrad 'Ideal factorization' Lemma 3.1, Thm 3.2, Thm 3.6; Gathmann Prop. 13.7

viewpoints.summary: Algebraic-geometric: Spec of a Dedekind domain is a regular (smooth) 1-dimensional scheme; the coordinate ring of a nonsingular affine curve is Dedekind; Pic(A) is the Picard group of the curve; for k[E] (elliptic curve minus origin) Pic = E(k).
viewpoints.source: Clark, Elliptic Dedekind domains revisited, §2.4; Gathmann Ex. 13.4(b), 13.29; Wikipedia

viewpoints.summary: Valuation-theoretic: nonzero primes of a Dedekind domain correspond to the discrete valuations of K that are nonnegative on A; in an extension, primes over p correspond to valuations of L extending v_p, with index e.

Arithmetic: rings of integers of number fields and global function fields; the class group is finite and every class contains infinitely many primes (Chebotarev / Hecke), unlike for general Dedekind domains.
viewpoints.source: Coykendall-Kettinger §4; Gargava et al. §2.2; Clark §2.3-2.4 (replete domains)

viewpoints.summary: Module-theoretic: Dedekind domains are the domains where invertible ideals are exactly the rank one projectives; finitely generated modules are torsion plus a projective part A^{n-1} + I, classified by rank and Steinitz class; Wikipedia also cites characterisation as hereditary domains.
viewpoints.source: Gargava et al. §2 Prop. 9; Wikipedia 'Dedekind domain' (modules); Milne Ch.3 'Modules over Dedekind domains (sketch)'

viewpoints.summary: Monoid/factorization-theoretic: a Dedekind domain is a Krull monoid of dimension <=1; the transfer homomorphism to zero-sum sequences over the class group shows arithmetic invariants (sets of lengths) depend only on Cl and the classes containing primes.

Formal/constructive: mathlib formalises three definitions and proves them equivalent; finiteness of class groups is proved uniformly for number and function fields via 'admissible absolute values', avoiding Minkowski.

conventions.summary: Fields: Stacks, Aitken, mathlib and Wikipedia count fields as Dedekind domains (vacuous conditions); Sutherland's AKLB setup and Gathmann's 'dimension 1' definition exclude them; Wikipedia notes many theorems need only trivial changes.
conventions.source: Stacks 10.120 (comments); Aitken Def. 1; Baanen §5.1; Gathmann Def. 13.1; Sutherland 2015 Lecture 5 setup

conventions.summary: Primary definition varies: unique ideal factorisation (Stacks, nLab); noetherian+integrally closed+dim<=1 (mathlib, Milne, Wikipedia DD4); DVR localisations (Sutherland); regular localisations (Gathmann); Krull of dim<=1 (Chang-Geroldinger).
conventions.source: Stacks Def. 10.120.14; nLab 'Dedekind domain'; Baanen §5.1; Sutherland Def. 2.10; Gathmann Def. 13.1; Chang-Geroldinger §2.2

conventions.summary: Fractional ideals: finitely generated submodule (Sutherland) vs submodule with common denominator (Conrad, Gathmann, mathlib); mathlib allows the zero fractional ideal with 0^{-1}=0, most texts require nonzero.
conventions.source: Sutherland Def. 2.13, Rem. 2.15; Baanen §5.2; Gathmann Def. 13.15

conventions.summary: Class group notation: cl(A) or Pic(A) (Sutherland), Pic R with Div R and Prin R (Gathmann), Cl_K, h_K (Coykendall-Kettinger), cl(K) (Gargava et al.), Pic(D) and Cl_v, Cl_t (Chang-Geroldinger), Cl O_K (Elsenhans-Voight). Group law written multiplicatively for ideals, additively in factorization theory.

Ideal norm: as a positive integer N(a)=|O_K/a| (Conrad, Elsenhans-Voight 'Nm') or as an ideal N_{B/A}(I) of A (Sutherland, relative case, defined via module index). Over Z they match by taking the positive generator.
conventions.source: Conrad 'Ideal factorization' §7; Sutherland 2015 Lecture 6 Def. 6.5, Prop. 6.11

conventions.summary: 'Prime' often means nonzero prime ideal; 'q | p' or 'q over p' means q contains pB, equivalently q intersect A = p. Unramified requires e=1 and separable residue extension (Sutherland); e,f,g notation with efg=n in Galois case.
conventions.source: Sutherland 2015 Lecture 5 setup, Def. 5.9, Lemma 5.1; Wikipedia 'Splitting of prime ideals'

conventions.summary: Class group vs narrow class group (positive generators), and ordinary vs ray class groups; Koymans-Pagano use both Cl and narrow Cl of quadratic fields.
conventions.source: Wikipedia 'Ideal class group'; Koymans-Pagano §1; Sutherland 2015 Lecture 20

examples.summary: Z[sqrt(-5)]: 6 = 2*3 = (1+sqrt(-5))(1-sqrt(-5)), 2 irreducible not prime; (2) = (2,1+sqrt(-5))^2, (3) = (3,1+sqrt(-5))(3,1-sqrt(-5)); (2,1+sqrt(-5)) non-principal because x^2+5y^2=2 has no solution; class group Z/2.
examples.source: Gathmann Ex. 13.6, 13.8, 13.28; Conrad 'Ideal factorization' Ex. 1.3, 2.8; Wikipedia 'Ideal class group'

examples.summary: PIDs (Z, k[x], Z[i]) and DVRs (Z_(p)) are Dedekind with trivial class group; k[x,y] is a UFD that is not Dedekind (dimension 2; (x,y) not invertible); Z[sqrt(-13)] is Dedekind but not a UFD.
examples.source: Sutherland Lecture 2 Cor. 2.11, Rem. 2.12; Gathmann Ex. 13.21(b); Baanen §5.2

examples.summary: Non-integrally-closed orders fail: in A = Z+2iZ the ideal 2Z[i] is not invertible; orders Z+pO_K violate contain=divide; only primes containing the conductor are non-invertible.
examples.source: Sutherland Lecture 2 Ex. 2.21; Conrad §8 Ex. 8.2; Sutherland 2015 Lecture 7 Thm 7.8

examples.summary: Z[sqrt(-3)] with p=(2,1+sqrt(-3)): p^2 = 2p, so p is not invertible (cancellation fails); its localisation at p is not a DVR. (Hand check: (1+w)^2 = -2+2w with w^2=-3.)
examples.source: seeds_localization.json exercise 3; computation checked by hand

examples.summary: Splitting in Z[i]: 2 = -i(1+i)^2 ramifies, p = 1 mod 4 splits (5=(2+i)(2-i), 13=(2+3i)(2-3i)), p = 3 mod 4 is inert with residue field F_{p^2}; sum e f = 2.
examples.source: Sutherland 2015 Lecture 5 example; Wikipedia 'Splitting of prime ideals in Galois extensions'

examples.summary: Q(zeta_5): f = x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1; 2 inert, 5 totally ramified (f = (x-1)^4 mod 5), 11 splits completely, 19 = two primes of residue degree 2.
Dedekind's cubic x^3-x^2-2x-8: 2 splits completely but [O_K:Z[alpha]] is even for every alpha, so no power basis works at 2 (first non-monogenic field); common index divisors.

Class group computations via Minkowski bound: Q(sqrt(-14)) and Q(sqrt(82)) cyclic of order 4, Q(sqrt(-30)) = (Z/2)^2, Q(sqrt(79)) order 3, Q(sqrt(-65)) = Z/2 x Z/4; class number 1 for Q(i), Q(sqrt(-2)), Q(sqrt(-3)), Q(sqrt(-7)), Q(sqrt 2), Q(sqrt 3), Q(sqrt 5), Q(sqrt 13).

Geometric: coordinate ring of smooth cubic y^2 = x(x-1)(x-lambda) is Dedekind, its Pic gives the chord-tangent group law; every abelian group is a class group (Claborn), even of an elliptic Dedekind domain (Clark).
Non-noetherian failure: the ring of all algebraic integers is not noetherian, hence not Dedekind (it is Bézout/Prüfer); almost Dedekind domains need not be Dedekind.
Localisations: Z[1/6] and Z_(p) Dedekind; semilocal Z_(3) intersect Z_(5) is a PID; Cl(D[1/alpha]) = Cl(D)/<classes of primes dividing alpha>.
examples.source: Sutherland Lecture 3 Ex. 3.20, Cor. 3.21; Coykendall-Kettinger Thm 4.1

computation.summary: Dedekind-Kummer: if B = A[alpha] (or more generally p prime to the conductor of A[alpha]) and the minimal polynomial factors mod p as prod g_i^{e_i}, then pB = prod (p, g_i(alpha))^{e_i} with f_i = deg g_i. Checkable sufficient condition: p does not divide disc(f).
computation.source: Sutherland 2015 Lecture 6 Thm 6.13, Prop. 6.16; Conrad 'Factoring after Dedekind' Thm 1, Cor. 4, Thm 8

computation.summary: When p divides the index, change generator, or use Ore/Montes higher Newton polygons with Hensel's lemma; common index divisors make every generator fail.
computation.source: Conrad 'Factoring after Dedekind' Ex. 5-7; Jakhar-Kaur-Kumar §2 Thm 2.6

computation.summary: Class group by hand: Minkowski bound; factor primes below it; find relations from norms N(a+b sqrt d) that are smooth; show non-principality by unsolvability of norm equations.
Class group by machine: factor base of primes up to Minkowski or Bach (GRH) bound, collect S-unit relations, Smith normal form of the relation matrix, verify with analytic class number formula.
Ideal norm: N(q) = p^{f_q}; N((alpha)) = (N_{L/K}(alpha)); N is multiplicative; N(IB) = I^n; over Z, N(a) = [O_K:a].
computation.source: Sutherland 2015 Lecture 6 Prop. 6.6-6.7, Thm 6.9, Cor. 6.10-6.11; Conrad 'Ideal factorization' §7

computation.summary: Valuation bookkeeping: compute ideal operations by exponents (sum = min, intersection = max, product = add); approximation theorem gives elements with prescribed valuations; second generator of I=(a,b) chosen by CRT.
computation.source: Sutherland Lecture 3 Lemma 3.16, Cor. 3.17, Thm 3.22; Gathmann Prop. 13.13

computation.summary: Sum e_i f_i = n via B/pB = prod B/q^{e}, each of dimension e f over A/p; in Galois extensions efg = n and decomposition/inertia groups have orders ef and e.
computation.source: Sutherland 2015 Lecture 5 Thm 5.7; Lecture 7 Cor. 7.15, Lemma 7.18, Prop. 7.22

computation.summary: Inverse of an ideal: I^{-1} = (A:I) = {x in K : xI in A}; for a prime p of O_K one has explicit inverses like (3,1+sqrt(-5))^{-1} = (1/3)(3,1-sqrt(-5)).

confusions.summary: Elements vs ideals: Dedekind domains are generally not UFDs; ideals factor uniquely, elements need not. Dedekind + UFD forces PID.
confusions.source: Sutherland Lecture 3 Cor. 3.15 and warnings; Aitken (intro); Gathmann Prop. 13.27

confusions.summary: Divisibility implies containment in any ring, but containment implies divisibility only in Dedekind domains (this property characterises them among noetherian domains).
confusions.source: Sutherland Lecture 3 warnings, Thm 3.23(5); Conrad Thm 4.3

confusions.summary: The set (A:I) is called I^{-1} but is a true inverse only if I is invertible; e.g. (X,Y) in C[X,Y], 2Z[i] in Z+2iZ.
Applying Dedekind-Kummer at a prime dividing the index gives wrong answers; for Q(sqrt 5) one must use x^2-x-1, not x^2-5, at p=2.
O_L need not be free over O_K when O_K is not a PID; monogenic is stronger than free; B_p in Sutherland means localisation as A-module (at the multiplicative set A minus p), not at a prime of B.
Every ideal class containing a prime is a theorem for rings of integers of global fields, not for all Dedekind domains (e.g. k[E] with k algebraically closed is not 'replete').
Integral closure of a Dedekind domain in an infinite algebraic extension need not be Dedekind (fails noetherianity); in a finite extension it is (Krull-Akizuki, no separability needed).
Prime terminology: Dedekind's 'prime ideals' are today's maximal ideals; in a Dedekind domain the nonzero primes are maximal, but (0) is a prime that is excluded from factorisations.
Math StackExchange and MathOverflow could not be reached in this session, so typical MSE confusions were not collected from those sites directly.

requirements.item: Definition(s) of Dedekind domain and their equivalence (noetherian+integrally closed+dim<=1; DVR localisations; invertible ideals; unique ideal factorisation)
Fractional ideals, (A:I), invertible ideals; nonzero fractional ideals of a Dedekind domain form a group, free abelian on nonzero primes
Unique factorisation of ideals; valuations v_p(I); contain=divide; gcd = sum, lcm = intersection
Ideal class group Cl/Pic, class number; Cl trivial iff PID iff UFD
Rings of integers O_K as Dedekind domains; integral closure of Dedekind domain in finite (separable) extension is Dedekind
Splitting of primes in extensions: pO_L = prod P^e, residue degree f, sum e_i f_i = n; ramified/inert/split
Ideal norm (absolute and relative), multiplicativity, N(P)=p^f, N((alpha)) = |N(alpha)|
Finiteness of the class group of O_K (Minkowski bound; or admissible absolute values)
Galois extensions: transitive action on primes over p, efg=n, decomposition and inertia groups, Frobenius
Dedekind-Kummer theorem and its index/conductor hypothesis; discriminant and index disc(f)=ind^2 d_K; ramified primes divide the discriminant
Localisation of Dedekind domains (S^{-1}D Dedekind, primes avoiding S, class group of localisation as quotient)
Examples: Z[sqrt(-5)] (class number 2), Z[i] splitting, PIDs, non-examples k[x,y], Z[sqrt(-3)], orders
Every ideal class contains (infinitely many) primes for rings of integers; equidistribution (Chebotarev/Hecke)
Every ideal two-generated; approximation theorem / CRT; every class contains an ideal prime to a given ideal
Finitely generated modules over Dedekind domains: torsion-free = A^{n-1}+I, Steinitz class; O_L need not be free over O_K
Orders, conductor, non-invertible primes, Pic of an order and its exact sequence to Pic(O_K)
Claborn's theorem (every abelian group is a class group); geometric Dedekind domains (smooth affine curves, Pic of elliptic curve)
Factorisation theory: Krull monoids, transfer to zero-sum sequences over Cl, half-factoriality (Carlitz h<=2), sets of lengths
Narrow class group, ray class groups and moduli, Hilbert class field (bridge to class field theory)
Computational: S-units, factor bases, Bach bound, Smith normal form, analytic class number formula; Ore/Montes when Dedekind-Kummer fails
Discrete valuations of K nonnegative on A correspond to nonzero primes; extensions of valuations correspond to primes above p
